title: The Muwatta
hookLine: the trodden path, one of the earliest books of law and hadith

lines: A PATH PRESSED FLAT BY FEET.
A NAME WITH THAT PICTURE IN IT.
cards: A path across open ground, pressed flat by feet until the walking is easy. Nobody laid it out with a ruler; people walking it made it.
Malik ibn Anas gave his book a name with that picture in it: al-Muwatta, usually translated the well-trodden path, or the path made smooth.

Not a new road cut by one man, but a road already walked: by the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, by his companions, by the people of Medina after them. Page by page, the book reads like a record of where those feet went.

teach.b: Tradition counts it among the earliest written books of Islamic law and hadith still in our hands. And it isn't only a list of hadith.

teach.h: ARRANGED BY TOPIC, LIKE A LAW BOOK.
teach.b: Malik arranges it by topic, the way a law book is: purity, prayer, fasting, pilgrimage, trade, marriage, and on through daily life.
Under each topic come sayings of the Prophet, then rulings of his companions, then what the people after them did, and often Malik's own comment: this is the practice among us here in Medina.
That phrase is tomorrow's whole lesson. How did it reach us?
Malik taught the book for years, and different students wrote down what they heard, so the Muwatta comes in more than one transmission.
The version of Yahya ibn Yahya al-Laythi, who carried it to Spain, is widely read today. Another comes through al-Shaybani, the Hanafi student from last week, who also studied with Malik.

Near the end, in the book on good character, Malik records that the Prophet said he was sent to perfect good character. A book of law, purity and trade, and close to its end, a line about who you are with people.
It's a fair summary of the path: the rules are walked so the person comes out better.

how: Muslims study the Muwatta of Imam Malik as a book of hadith and law, and in Maliki lands it has long been taught in mosques and schools, usually in the transmission of Yahya ibn Yahya al-Laythi.

Malik's city, where the Prophet lived and was buried

games.q: a book of purity, prayer, trade and marriage. near its end, in the book on good character, what line does Malik record?
o: that only scholars may read the law.
that the Prophet was sent to perfect good character.
that trade should be left to others.
games.why: he was sent to perfect good character. the rules are walked so the person comes out better.

practice: Say the line from the book on good character slowly, once: the Prophet said that he was sent to perfect good character.

Then picture a path your feet know, from your front door to somewhere you go every day, and ask what one small piece of good character would look like, walked that often: a greeting at the same door, a thank-you to the same driver.
If you pray, you can carry the line into your prayer.

wordCard.voice: The Muwatta. Malik's book of law and hadith, arranged by topic; its name is usually translated the well-trodden path. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the trodden, the made-smooth; Malik's book of law and hadith.

carryVoice: Your line: the well-trodden path. Good character, walked often enough, becomes the road. Until tomorrow.
